[quote=qianxun;60345319][b]Hold your breath[/b]

"Here's water." Kang Hongxin points to the open lake, one arm straight through the great horizon. "The wuxing tells us five elements: Wood, fire, earth, metal, water. Water overcomes fire and is overcome by earth."

The ship then stopped, and Kang leaned forward, while the three divers nearly fell to the ground in a collective thud. Beneath them, Qianxun Lake Major stared menacingly, its waters steadily intensifying its movements into waves. Kang only smirked and tossed the three men their raincoats as he pointed down into the searing current. Each scrambled to shield themselves from the sudden rising and falling of the waves.

"This boat is metal." Kang says calmly. "And in the five elements, metal creates and overacts upon water, like how we use metal buckets to collect water. But if metal is used in excess? Like, say, I dunno... a gigantic research vessel intruding upon a sensitive domain? Well, heh..."

As if on cue, water began to pile onto the deck of the ship, accumulating, then draining as they flow out through the scuppers. A ferocious wind moved into the lake and whispered into their ears. "The lake wants us to leave." Kang joked, but one of the men laughed. Perhaps they took the jest to heart, or perhaps the rocking of the waves against their little research vessel left much to be desired. But Kang's expression never changed, never faded from a detached apathy from the fury of the waves, rather keeping to the wonders of his tall tales. The three divers listened on.

"Qianxun Major is an angry dragon, folks. She does not like it when we intrude upon her domain, but don't worry about a thing."

"What makes you say that, Director?"

"She's just being shy." Kang chuckled. "Well, what're you waiting for? Suit up!"

The order was given. The men paled, but the Director-General's seemingly bored demanor overtook any authority of the great waves. Kang walked with the men to the dive locker and sat each man down by the modules for their gear. These were not simple wetsuits; such simplicities will kill a man entering the dragon's lair. What they needed was the pinnacle of human technology, that could brave the terror of the waves.

"Water overcomes fire." Kang reminded them. "So don't screw up the hot water suits. Don't screw up anything, but especially not the hot water. Water overcomes fire. Go down there with a misplaced suit, and the water will freeze you to death."

This "hot water suit" Kang described, it was like an overized long john. Like a wet suit but with thin plastic tubing woven into the fabric. These tubes lined their entire bodies and were connected to a hot water supply on the ship that was to keep them nice and warm in the frigid abyss. The temperatures deep below reached freezing, and they were meant to work there for an hour at a time.

"And this one, Comrade Kang?" a diver asked, pointing to the large, astronaut-like suits that stood prominently in the dive locker.

"Those are what makes divers aquanauts." Kang coolly replied. "Earth overcomes water. Dams channel or restrain water flow. And in the world beneath the world, we must restrain. The pressure down there dissolves nitrogen and helium into our blood and veins, but it also crushes us. This shell protects those who dare go where humans were never designed to go."

Kang took one of the empty suits. On its arms indicated its purpose, written in Latin text: ATMOSPHERIC DIVING SUIT, or ADS for short. Kangs men assisted each diver, sealing them into the rigid, anthropomorphic metal exoskeleton one limb at a time. Perhaps this is what coined the term aquanauts, for their dense armor and robotic gait seemed more fitting so far above than here down below.

Next, the umbilical cord. The "lifeline". A long, thick, cable-packed hose containing heliox, hot water, power for the suit lights, comms, and a fiber-optic video link. Attached to the ADS, attached to the ship. The three aquanauts were now physically tethered to life itself.

The men waddled like penguins away from the main deck and deeper into the heart of their research vessel. QNS Hai Xia, they called this ship, whose name meant "Sea Champion". Her hull creaked as the waves shattered against her frame, but did not list, did not waver. The men walked deeper down into the vessel and towards a yellow-painted structure stretching outwards into the starboard side of the Hai Xia. HYPERBARIC CHAMBER, it was written, in bright red text to remain visible even to the drunken, lame eye.

It seemed like a barracks inside, or perhaps a more luxurious prison. All around them, visible metal and piping. A few beds stacked perhaps too closely together. Desks for work, waterproof computers no better in performance from devices a decade ago, a router bolted into the ceiling, another separate compartment for relieving waste. Kang locked the chamber shut behind them, and the men shuddered. A quiet hiss and whisper, and pressure began to build up in the chamber.

"It's like a tight hug that takes a second too long." Kang joked, but only one or two men chuckled. Soon enough, the chamber was now to the same level of pressure as the absolute abyss. Whether they were down there working the lake or up here resting or going about their day, the pressure remained the same. There would be no risk of decompression.

The men walked with Kang to the hatch built into the bottom of the hyperbaric chamber. It was like having a manhole embedded into your own bedroom. The chamber stuck out to the side of the Hai Xia, and this hatch stuck out bottom of the chamber. Like sets of exterior appendages, one growing out of the other. Kang opened the hatch and led the men deeper in, but does not go in himself. His task was to oversee the operation from the comforts of the computer, not down there together with them.

In the mean time, the men explored, or tried to explore, the tiny chamber that awaited beyond the hatch.

This was the bell, the elevator of the Hai Xia, which they were to use each and every time they were to descend into the depths below. Unlike the hyperbaric chamber above, this bell was not meant for casual living. It walls were too claustrophobic, if the aquanauts did not immediately notice the complete absence of amenities. "Sit tight and enjoy the ride." Kang remarked through their comms. "Oh, and comms check. Loud and clear, ain't I?"

"Loud and clear, Comrade Kang." said one aquanaut, before suddenly jumping. His voice was now squeaky, like a mouse.

"Audio is good." affirmed another, chuckling at his own voice. "Damned heliox."

"Good."

Following Kang's instructions, the men found a good place to sit inside the bell. Then, each diver detached his umbilical cord from the main ship, but just for a moment, and instead would plug them into an internal panel embedded deep within the bell itself. A hiss, a thunk, and the bell is sealed. Then, it began to descend, freeing itself from its fusion into the main hyperbaric chamber and releasing into the moonpool at the bottom of the Hai Xia.

It was like the compromise between an elevator ride and freefall. The bell lowered into the waters, guided by a winch and rope aboard the mother ship. At first, light still pierced through the shallow waters, and the men could see what regular divers and swimmers could see. Carps, pikes, and bitterlings wade through the blue-green waters, mostly trying to flee the bell that was rapidly cruising through towards them.

Within the first hundred meters, the world began to change. 

The blue-green world transitioned to a lonely, dark blue. The Sun, once a beautiful plate of gold, began ti dissipate into a distant coin, its light struggling to reach them. The familiar fish vanished, replaced by sleek, shadowy forms with eyes built for the gloom. A pale, ghostly squid, all arms and tentacles, pulsed past a viewport, jetting away into the nothingness.

Five hundred meters. 

Half a kilometer later, and they had reached the world before twilight. Blue turned to black, the bell's external lights snaped on, the men began to shudder. Starting from here was the domain of the unknown, which no man was ever designed to reach. A gulper eel, a creature little more than a mouth attached to a long, whiplike tail, drifted by, its jaw unhinged in a perpetual gasp at the absurdity of its own form. Occasionally, the bell's lights might catch the shimmering, internal-organ glow of a fragile, gelatinous jellyfish, a [i]ctenophore[/i], beating with iridescent cilia like a living, pulsating galaxy.

One kilometer. 

What remained of the Sun was now gone. Water overcomes fire. They were now in the abyssal depths, a world of absolute blackness, where light could not possibly penetrate, and colder than any winter storm. "Life here stops making sense." Kang chattered through the comms, telling the men to keep their eyes peeled at what lay ahead. A fangtooth fish, with faces writ upon a nightmare's creativity, bristling with teeth too large for their own heads, were lured to the lights before darting away. The infamous anglerfish, a sedentary female with a glowing lure swaying from her forehead, peered ominously into the bell's window before disappearing.

A kilometer and a half. 

Life became more alien still.  The pressure here was unimaginable, yet life persisted in strange, often sluggish forms. Ghostly white amphipods, like giant swimming lice, scuttled at the edge of the light. Sea pigs, ethereal and pale, seemed to crawl on the void itself. The water was filled with a constant, slow snowfall of "marine snow"the decaying detritus of the world above, falling endlessly to feed the creatures of the deep.

"Earth overcomes water." Kangs voice crackled over the comm, his tone unchanged. "This is the world beneath the world, gentlemen. Down here, water is truth. These creatures do not know the sun and do not know the world that we ourselves have lived. Whatever you see now is not a result of a million, million years of adaptation, but sacred design. Earth overcomes water. See the snow? Earth feeds these things. And they go on about their day, not understanding the sheer pressure of the water that was crushing down on them."

"Is this the deepest we'll go?" one aquanaut asked nervously.

"No." Kang bluntly responded. "The voice is further down."

The bell continued its descent, the creatures outside becoming rarer, more cryptic, more ancient. The beams of light now seemed to push against a palpable darkness, a pressure not just physical, but psychological. "Astronauts have it lucky." one aquanaut joked. "Least they've star to look at."

Nervous laughter, nervous shivers. The men hold their breaths as the bell kept descending. Then, a thud.

"Earth overcomes water." Kang reminded them as the aquanauts prepared to unlock the hatch. "You three are now extensions of the earth that will walk across the lakebed. You cannot be overcome by water who becomes hardened like the mountains and fjords. Hesitate for a moment, and you die."

The three aquanauts nodded at Kang's instruction, then to each other.

"Open the hatch."[/quote]
